```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

This vignette walks through the metrictrails pipeline with the files shipped
in the package: a trail run on Manquehue hill (Santiago, Chile) recorded by a
GNSS watch, the same loop drawn as a route, and a small Digital Elevation
Model (DEM) of the area.

```{r setup}
library(metrictrails)

activity_file = system.file("extdata", "gpx_activity.gpx", package = "metrictrails")
route_file = system.file("extdata", "gpx_route.gpx", package = "metrictrails")
dem_file = system.file("extdata", "test_dem.tif", package = "metrictrails")
```

The pipeline has five steps:

1. **ingest** a GPX file, `read_stream()`;
2. apply the **naming convention**, `uniform_stream()`;
3. **sanitize** the coordinates, `sanitize_stream()`;
4. **resample** to a uniform spatial resolution, `resample_stream()`;
5. replace the **elevation** with values from a DEM, `ele_correction()`.

## 1. Ingest

`read_stream()` reads the track points of a GPX file with sf. Every track
segment becomes a value of `segment`, and Garmin point extensions (heart rate,
cadence, temperature) become numeric columns.

```{r}
raw = read_stream(activity_file)
raw
```

## 2. Naming convention

`uniform_stream()` renames the columns to `lon`, `lat`, `ele`, `timestamp` and
`time` (seconds since the start). It also works on data frames from other
sources, such as the Strava API streams in `strava_streams`.

```{r}
raw = uniform_stream(raw)
names(raw)
head(uniform_stream(strava_streams), 3)
```

## 3. Sanitize

`sanitize_stream()` first flags readings that are physically implausible:
speed, acceleration, jumps at the edges, slope, vertical speed, and elevation
changes while the athlete stands still. Then it smooths `lon` and `lat`. The
default method is a constant-velocity Kalman filter with a
Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother; LOESS, a Gaussian kernel, Savitzky-Golay and the
full post-processing pipeline of Martinez, Sanchez & Diaz (2026) are also
available.

```{r}
clean = sanitize_stream(raw)
attr(clean, "sanitize_report")$counts
```

The flags are computed on the raw readings, before smoothing. In this
activity the positions raise no flags. The flags concern the raw elevation:
slopes above 50 degrees between close readings, implausible vertical speeds,
and elevation changes while standing still. Flagged readings can be kept
(`action = "flag"`, the default), dropped or interpolated.

```{r}
methods = c("kalman", "loess", "gaussian", "savgol", "pipeline")
lengths = sapply(methods, function(m) {
  summarise_stream(sanitize_stream(raw, method = m))$distance_2d
})
round(c(raw = summarise_stream(raw)$distance_2d, lengths))
```

Every method removes part of the positional noise, which shortens the path.
LOESS with its default span smooths the most.

## 4. Resample: the Nyquist resolution

A watch that records every second produces a spatial resolution that is a
random variable: the distance between readings is the speed times the
sampling interval. Because trails are fractal, distance and elevation gain
depend on that resolution (Sanchez et al., 2025), so two recordings of the
same trail are not directly comparable.

`resolution_stream()` describes the distribution of the horizontal distance
between moving readings:

```{r}
resolution_stream(clean)
```

Its 0.9 quantile, `res`, is the finest uniform spacing that represents the
path without inventing readings between sparse fixes. `resample_stream()`
uses it by default:

```{r}
resampled = resample_stream(clean)
attr(resampled, "res")
nrow(resampled)
```

The fractal effect is easy to see by resampling the same stream at increasing
resolutions:

```{r fractal}
res = c(1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 30, 50, 80)
distance = sapply(res, function(r) summarise_stream(resample_stream(clean, res = r))$distance_2d)
plot(res, distance / 1000, log = "x", type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Resolution (m, log scale)", ylab = "Distance (km)")
abline(v = attr(resampled, "res"), lty = 2)
```

To compare several streams, resample all of them with one common resolution,
at least the largest of their Nyquist resolutions:

```{r}
streams = list(activity = clean, route = read_stream(route_file))
resolution_stream(streams)[, c("stream", "q50", "res")]
common = max(resolution_stream(streams)$res)
```

The route was drawn with sparse vertices, so it sets the common resolution.

`fractal_stream()` summarises the same behaviour as a fractal dimension
(divider method):

```{r}
fd = fractal_stream(clean)
fd$dimension
```

## 5. Elevation from a DEM

Raw elevation comes from a barometer or from GNSS, and it is noisy and often
rounded to the metre. `ele_correction()` replaces it with values from a DEM.
Without a `dem` argument, `get_dem()` downloads AWS Terrain Tiles at zoom 14
along a corridor around the stream. Here we use the DEM shipped with the
package:

```{r}
final = ele_correction(resampled, dem = dem_file)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# same result with a downloaded DEM, refined to 1 m by bilinear interpolation
dem = get_dem(resampled, res = 1)
final = ele_correction(resampled, dem = dem)
```

```{r elevation}
d_raw = differential_stream(raw)
d_final = differential_stream(final)
plot(d_raw$distance / 1000, raw$ele, type = "l", col = "grey60",
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Elevation (m)")
lines(d_final$distance / 1000, final$ele, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", c("device", "pipeline + DEM"), col = c("grey60", "black"), lwd = c(1, 1.5), bty = "n")
```

## Measures

`differential_stream()` adds per-reading differences and rates, and
`summarise_stream()` the course-level measures, here before and after the
pipeline:

```{r}
cols = c("distance_2d", "elevation_gain", "elevation_loss", "km_effort", "resolution")
cbind(stream = c("raw", "pipeline"),
      rbind(summarise_stream(raw)[, cols], summarise_stream(final)[, cols]))
```

### Tobler parameters

`tobler_stream()` fits an asymmetric Tobler hiking function to the
speed-slope relation. It models the frontier of performance (by default the
0.9 quantile of speed), not the mean, by minimising the quantile loss.

```{r tobler}
params = tobler_stream(final)
params

d = differential_stream(final)
keep = is.finite(d$speed) & is.finite(d$slope) & abs(d$slope) <= 0.6
plot(d$slope[keep], d$speed[keep], pch = 16, cex = 0.4, col = "grey60",
     xlab = "Slope (rise over run)", ylab = "Horizontal speed (m/s)")
slope = seq(-0.6, 0.6, by = 0.01)
lines(slope, tobler_speed(slope, params), lwd = 2)
```

In this single activity the frontier is flat downhill (`c_minus` close to 0)
and the speed only drops on steep climbs. Many activities, or a population
of athletes, give a better-defined frontier.

## Two streams

`detect_stream()` is a predicate: does the activity follow the route, in
which direction, and between which readings?

```{r}
route = read_stream(route_file)
detect_stream(raw, route)
```

`locate_stream()` projects every reading on the route (linear referencing),
and `compare_stream()` measures the spatial agreement of two streams
resampled at the same resolution:

```{r}
located = locate_stream(clean, route)
summary(abs(located$offset_cross))

compare_stream(resample_stream(clean, res = 2), resample_stream(route, res = 2))
```

### Matching to a known reference

When the athlete is known to have followed a reference trail, for example
rounds on a trail measured with a high-precision protocol, `match_stream()`
estimates where the athlete was along the reference at every timestamp. The
match never moves backwards and never exceeds the Tobler ceiling, and the
global optimum is found by dynamic programming. The result keeps the time and
the other variables of the stream, takes the coordinates and elevation of the
reference, and reports the offset of every reading along and across the
trail.

```{r}
reference = route %>% resample_stream(res = 2) %>% ele_correction(dem = dem_file)
matched = match_stream(clean[1:800, ], reference, params = params)
attr(matched, "match_report")
summary(matched[, c("offset_d", "offset_along", "offset_cross")])
```

```{r matched}
plot(matched$time / 60, matched$s_ref / 1000, type = "l",
     xlab = "Time (min)", ylab = "Position along the reference (km)")
```

## Writing the result

```{r}
out = tempfile(fileext = ".gpx")
write_stream(final, out, name = "Manquehue loop")
nrow(read_stream(out))
```

## References

* Sanchez, R., & Villena, M. (2020). Comparative evaluation of wearable devices for measuring elevation gain in mountain physical activities. *Proc IMechE Part P*, 234(4), 312-319. <https://doi.org/10.1177/1754337120918975>
* Sanchez, R., Egli, P., Besomi, M., & Truffello, R. (2024). Assessing the impact of Digital Elevation Model resolution on elevation gain estimations in trail running. *ICECET 2024*. <https://doi.org/10.1109/ICECET61485.2024.10698606>
* Sanchez, R., Egli, P. E., Jornet, K., Duggan, M., & Besomi, M. (2025). How fractal complexity distorts distance and elevation gain in trail and mountain running. *Proc IMechE Part P*. <https://doi.org/10.1177/17543371251341660>
* Sanchez, R., Nieto-Jimenez, C., & Riveros-Matthey, C. (2025). High-precision mapping of mountain terrain for human locomotion research. *ICPRS 2025*. <https://doi.org/10.1109/ICPRS66293.2025.11302827>
* Martinez, C., Sanchez, R., & Diaz, C. (2026). A post-processing methodology for improving kinematic consistency in GNSS-based running trajectories. *ICECET 2026*. <https://doi.org/10.1109/ICECET65726.2026.11632531>
